lines.text: This is Atlas. A small box that sits on your desk, with two camera eyes.
It watches your space, remembers what it saw, answers your questions, and learns new skills. All of it on the box. Your video never leaves.

Inside are four layers. Cameras, with every face blurred before anything is saved. A vision model that understands the scene. A memory of everything it saw. And an agent that never acts without asking you first.
Everything after this minute is something you point Atlas at. Pick your track, press the key, and watch two minutes.
Point it at your week. Atlas reads your classes and deadlines, and watches how your day really goes at the desk.
Each morning it writes one plan, with its reasons. When something slips, it re-plans. In the evening, it tells you what happened against the plan.
Nothing is written to your calendar until you tap approve.
The model on the box is small. That is what makes it private and fast. But small models have gaps.
When Atlas needs a new skill, you tap teach. It asks to export a handful of blurred pictures. A big open model in the lab labels them, and the small one is fine-tuned on the answers.
A test decides if the new model is really better. Only then does it ship back to the box. Our adapter is public on Hugging Face.
The lab is two AMD Radeon R9700 cards. One serves the teacher, a twenty-seven billion parameter Qwen. The other trains.
Labeling, training, testing and packaging run on ROCm, and every run is recorded, with its loss curve, its minutes and its watts.
The box and the lab share two files, a dataset out and a model package back. Nothing else crosses.
The new model arrives as one small package. The box checks it, swaps it in, and rolls back by itself if it does not answer.
We measure energy on both sides. Watts on the Jetson, watts on the GPUs, and joules per answer, so you can see what a question costs.
Everything you see live runs on this Jetson. Cameras in, faces blurred, the on-device vision model understanding the scene, answers in a few seconds.
Pull the network cable. It keeps seeing, remembering, alerting and answering. Only learning pauses.
The same cameras turn a room into data. Frames become events. Events become episodes you can ask about.
Point it at the bins, and it counts what gets thrown away and where it lands.
With a count comes a number a campus can act on. How much was sorted right, before and after a nudge.
Tables share only their counts, never their pictures, and a leaderboard shows who is winning.
Point it at your friends. Each person's Atlas keeps their own calendar private.
Ask for a time that works for everyone, and the boxes negotiate. Only free or busy leaves each box. The event lands in everyone's plan after a tap.
Point it at your habits. Day Run lets you play tomorrow before you live it, on a map of your own campus.
A bad plan fails, and the game tells you why. A good plan wins three stars. Hard mode moves a class and makes you re-route.
It is the same box, the same cameras, the same memory. Pointed at one more part of your life.
